text: Gerhard Richter, born on 9 February 1932 in Dresden-Neustadt, Saxony, is a German visual artist known for his abstract and photorealistic paintings, photographs, and glass pieces. He is widely regarded as one of the most important contemporary German artists, with several of his works setting record auction prices, and he was once the most expensive living painter. Richter has been described as the "greatest living painter," "the world's most important artist," and "the Picasso of the 21st century." He grew up in Reichenau (now Bogatynia, Poland) and Waltersdorf (Zittauer Gebirge), where his father, Horst Richter, was a mathematics and physics student at the Technische Hochschule in Dresden, and his mother, Hildegard Schönfelder, gave birth to him at 25; her father, Ernst Alfred Schönfelder, was once considered a gifted pianist. After Ernst moved the family to Dresden for a brewing enterprise that eventually went bankrupt, Hildegard trained as a bookseller and developed a passion for literature and music. Horst joined the National Socialist Party in Reichenau, though he remained apolitical and was not required to attend rallies; Gerhard was conscripted into the Hitler Youth at age 10, but the organization was dissolved before he reached enlistment age. In 1943, Hildegard moved the family to Waltersdorf and later sold her piano; two of her brothers died in the war, and her sister, Gerhard's aunt Marianne, who had schizophrenia, was starved to death in a psychiatric clinic as a victim of the Nazi euthanasia program. Richter left school after the 10th grade and apprenticed as an advertising and stage-set painter, completing vocational high school in Zittau in 1948. Between 1949 and 1951, he worked as an apprentice with a sign painter and as a painter, though his application to the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts in 1950 was rejected as "too bourgeois." He began studying at the Academy in 1951 under teachers Karl von Appen, Heinz Lohmar, and Will Grohmann. From 1957 to 1961, he worked as a master trainee, producing murals such as Arbeiterkampf (Workers' Struggle), portraits of East German actress Angelica Domröse and his first wife Ema, self-portraits, and a panorama of Dresden titled Stadtbild (Townscape, 1956). In 1957, he married Marianne Eufinger, who gave birth to his first daughter; he married sculptor Isa Genzken in 1982 and had two sons and a daughter with his third wife, Sabine Moritz, whom he married in 1995. In the early 1950s, he created a wall painting titled Communion with Picasso (1955) for the Academy's refectory and another, Lebensfreude (Joy of Life), for the German Hygiene Museum, intended to resemble wallpaper or tapestry. Both murals were later painted over for ideological reasons in East Germany; after reunification, parts of Joy of Life were uncovered in 2024, though earlier uncovered sections were covered during a restoration to the museum’s original 1930 state. In West Germany, Richter studied at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf under Karl Otto Götz alongside Sigmar Polke, Werner Hilsing, HA Schult, Kuno Gonschior, Franz Erhard Walther, Konrad Lueg, and Gotthard Graubner. With Polke and Konrad Fischer (pseudonym Lueg), he introduced the term Kapitalistischer Realismus (Capitalistic Realism) as an anti-style, appropriating advertising imagery and critiquing both Socialist Realism and Western consumer-driven art. He taught at the Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg and the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design as a visiting professor and returned to the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in 1971, where he taught for over 15 years. In 1983, he moved to Cologne, where he still lives and works, and in 1996, he moved into a studio designed by architect Thiess Marwede. During the 1960s and early 1970s, he created paintings from black-and-white photographs based on newspapers, books, private snapshots, aerial views, seascapes, and a large multipart work for the 1972 Venice Biennale. For Forty-eight Portraits (1971–72), he painted faces of composers like Gustav Mahler and Jean Sibelius and writers such as H. G. Wells and Franz Kafka. From around 1964, he made portraits of dealers, collectors, and artists, including two of his daughter Betty (1977 and 1988) and three titled IG (1993) of his second wife, Isa Genzken; Lesende (1994) depicts Sabine Moritz reading a magazine. Many of his realist paintings reflect on Nazi history, including depictions of family members who were members or victims of the regime. From 1966, he began using photographs he took himself as the basis for portraits. In 1975, for a Düsseldorf show, Gilbert & George commissioned a portrait from him. Richter began making prints in 1965, producing over 100 works between 1965 and 1974 using screenprint, photolithography, and collotype to achieve a "non-art" appearance, and stopped in 1974, beginning instead to paint from photographs he took. Early landscape elements appeared in 1963, but he began a distinct series of landscapes in 1968 after a vacation in Corsica. These works are compared to Caspar David Friedrich and are rooted in traditional German Romantic painting. Große Teyde-Landschaft (1971) draws from holiday snapshots of Tenerife. Atlas, first exhibited in 1972 at the Museum voor Hedendaagse Kunst in Utrecht with 315 parts, expanded and was later shown in full at the Lenbachhaus in Munich (1989), Museum Ludwig in Cologne (1990), and Dia Art Foundation in New York (1995); it continues as an ongoing work with approximately 4,000 photographs, reproductions, or cut-outs on about 600 panels. In 1972, Richter traveled to Greenland alone, intending to document the arctic landscape; in 1976, four large paintings titled Seascape emerged from those photographs. In 1982 and 1983, he created a series of Candles and Skulls still lifes, inspired by vanitas painters like Georges de La Tour and Francisco de Zurbarán, based on studio photographs, with only 27 works made; in 1995, he created a monumental solitary candle over the River Elbe to mark the 50th anniversary of the Allied bombing of Dresden. He described the series as evoking feelings of contemplation, memory, silence, and death. In 1988, he produced 15 ambiguous photo paintings titled 18 October 1977 depicting members of the Red Army Faction (RAF), based on black-and-white newspaper and police photos, including official portraits, arrest photos, prison images, and funeral scenes of Meinhof, Ensslin, Baader, and Jan-Carl Raspe. Since 1989, he has created new images by dragging wet paint over photographs, mostly snapshots of daily life. In 2001, Richter was flying to New York on 11 September but was diverted to Halifax due to the 9/11 attacks; a few years later, he made a small painting about the attacks. In his 2005 painting September, Robert Storr situates it within an anti-ideological framework, comparing it to the 18 October 1977 series regarding photographic documentation and memory. In the 2000s, he created works on scientific phenomena; in 2003, he produced several paintings titled Silicate, depicting latticed rows of light- and dark-grey blobs based on a photo from the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung of computer-generated reflections from silicon dioxide in insects' shells. In 2014, he created a cycle of four paintings titled Birkenau using Sonderkommando photographs from Auschwitz-Birkenau, which were made permanently available to the International Auschwitz Committee in October 2021 and are on permanent display in a pavilion near Auschwitz II-Birkenau, designed by Richter. In 2024, an edition of the Birkenau works as prints on metal plate, made and donated by Richter, went on display at the Centre. His early work Table (1962) combined a magazine photograph of a table with tachiste gestural marks in grey paint, canceling the photorealism and introducing generativity. In 1969, he produced the first of a group of grey monochromes using only textures from paint application. In 1976, he first titled a work Abstract Painting, emphasizing an accidental, unexplained process over creation. His abstract works build up layers of non-representational paint, beginning with broad strokes of primary color, evolving through spontaneous gestures, and using techniques like blurring and scraping to veil and expose prior layers. From the mid-1980s, he began using a homemade squeegee to rub and scrape paint in large bands, and in the 1990s, he ran the squeegee up and down to create vertical columns resembling a wall of planks. His abstract works, despite their unnatural palettes and lack of spatial depth, often appear as windows to an external landscape, equalizing illusion and paint. In the 1990s, he began a cycle of over 2,000 overpainted photographs, including Firenze, which consists of 99 small paintings of Florence created as a tribute to Steve Reich and the Contempoartensemble. After 2000, he continued creating works on scientific phenomena, particularly those involving aspects of reality invisible to the naked eye. In 2006, he continued this exploration.

Despite unnatural palettes, spaceless sheets of color, and visible trails of the artist's tools, Gerhard Richter's abstract paintings often function like windows, allowing viewers to perceive an external landscape. This effect parallels his representational works, where worldly images are reduced to mere incidents of art; similarly, in his abstract pieces, Richter elevates spontaneous, intuitive mark-making to a level of spatial logic and believability. Firenze is a series of 99 small paintings created in the autumn of 1999 and executed in that year and beyond, depicting the city of Florence as a tribute to the music of Steve Reich and the Contempoartensemble, a Florence-based musical group. This series belongs to the broader body of overpainted photographs, or übermalte Fotographien, which includes more than 2,000 works. After 2000, Richter produced works exploring scientific phenomena, particularly those invisible to the naked eye. In 2006, he created six paintings titled Cage, named after American avant-garde composer John Cage, using large canvases with intersecting fields, lines, and uneven smears generated by dragging a squeegee tool and removing paint to reveal layered, variegated patches. In May 2002, Richter photographed 216 details from his abstract painting no. 648-2 (1987), 10 x 15 cm in size, and combined them with 165 texts from the German newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (published on 20 and 21 March) to produce a 2004 book titled War Cut. In November 2008, Richter began a series applying ink droplets to wet paper, using alcohol and lacquer to control ink bloom and creep, resulting in double-sided works; sometimes upper sheets bled into others, forming sequential images, and in some cases, lacquer was applied to one side or pencil lines were drawn across color patches. As early as 1966, Richter created paintings based on color charts, drawing inspiration from found objects that arranged colored rectangles in limitless hues. His experiments culminated in 1973–74 with large-format works such as 256 Colours. Between 1966 and 1974, he produced three series of Color Chart works, each growing more ambitious in its attempt to generate meaning through arbitrary color arrangements. His first series began in 1966 with a small painting entitled 10 Colors, where he used his friend Blinky Palermo to randomly call out colors, introducing chance into the process. In the 1970s, Richter shifted focus from readymade objects to conceptual systems, developing mathematical procedures for mixing primary colors in graduated amounts and using chance operations to determine color placement. His second series of Color Charts began in 1971 and consisted of five paintings. In the final series from 1973–1974, additional elements were introduced, including light grey, dark grey, and later green. Richter's 4900 Colours from 2007 features bright monochrome squares randomly arranged in a grid, creating kaleidoscopic fields; it consists of 196 panels in 25 colors, reassembled in 11 variations, including a version with 49 paintings measuring 97 by 97 centimeters, developed specifically for the Serpentine Gallery. Richter began using glass in 1967 with Four Panes of Glass, which could tilt at varying angles. In 1970, he and Blinky Palermo jointly proposed a design for the 1972 Munich Olympic Games arena featuring 27 different colored glass windows, each appearing fifty times, distributed randomly. In 1981, for a two-person show with Georg Baselitz in Düsseldorf, Richter created the first of his monumental transparent mirrors, larger than his paintings and featuring adjustable steel mounts; for pieces like Mirror Painting (Grey, 735-2) (1991), the glass was colored grey by coating the back with pigment. At Documenta 9 in Kassel in 1992, Richter presented an ensemble of paintings and colored mirrors in a pavilion designed with architect Paul Robbrecht. In 2002, for the Dia Art Foundation, Richter created a glass sculpture including Spiegel I and Spiegel II (1989), measuring 7 feet tall and 18 feet long, which alters the gallery environment and visual experience, and Kugel (Sphere) (1992), a stainless steel mirror reflecting space. Since 2002, he has produced three-dimensional glass constructions such as 6 Standing Glass Panels (2002/2011). In 2010, the Drawing Center presented Lines which do not exist, a survey of Richter's drawings from 1966 to 2005, including works made with mechanical intervention like a pencil attached to an electric hand drill; it was the first U.S. career overview since the 2002 MoMA retrospective. R. H. Lossin wrote in The Brooklyn Rail that Richter's drawing practice documented a hand that couldn't draw properly, displacing the artist's hand with material evidence of failure. Throughout his career, Richter has declined lucrative licensing deals and private commissions. A 1968 commission from Siemens, Domplatz, Mailand (9 by 9.5 feet), depicting the Milan Duomo and Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, hung in Siemens offices in Milan from 1968 to 1998 and was sold by Sotheby's in London in 1998 for $3.6 million. In 1980, Richter and Isa Genzken were commissioned to design the König-Heinrich-Platz underground station in Duisburg, completed in 1992. In 1986, he received commissions for two large-scale paintings, Victoria I and Victoria II, from the Victoria insurance company in Düsseldorf. In 1990, he co-created works for the Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechselbank in Düsseldorf with Sol LeWitt and Oswald Mathias Ungers. In 1998, he installed a wall piece based on Germany's flag in the rebuilt Reichstag in Berlin. In 2012, he designed the first page of the German newspaper Die Welt. In 2017, he designed the label for the 2015 Chateau Mouton Rothschild's first wine. In 2002, Richter was commissioned to design a stained glass window for Cologne Cathedral, unveiled in August 2007; it is an 113 square meter (1,220 sq ft) abstract collage of 11,500 pixel-like squares in 72 colors, randomly arranged by computer (with some symmetry), reminiscent of his 1974 painting 4096 Colours. He waived any fee, and the costs—around €370,000 ($506,000)—were covered by donations from over 1,000 people. Cardinal Joachim Meisner did not attend the unveiling, preferring a figurative depiction of 20th-century Christian martyrs, stating the window would fit better in a mosque or prayer house; Richter, a professed atheist with a strong leaning toward Catholicism, had his three children baptized in the Cologne Cathedral. In September 2020, Richter unveiled three 30-foot-tall stained-glass windows for Tholey Abbey, one of Germany's oldest monasteries, which he called his last major work, after which he would focus on drawings and sketches. The windows were made by Gustva van Treeck in Munich and are abstract painted works inspired by his "Pattern" series from the 1990s. An additional 34 figurative stained-glass windows by Afghan-German Muslim artist Mahbuba Maqsoodi are expected to be completed by Easter 2021. The monks hoped the windows would promote tourism and bring people into faith. Richter first exhibited in Düsseldorf in 1963 and had his first gallery solo show in 1964 at Galerie Schmela in Düsseldorf. Soon after, he exhibited in Munich and Berlin, and by the early 1970s, he exhibited frequently throughout Europe and the United States. In 1966, Bruno Bischofberger was the first to show Richter's works outside Germany. His first retrospective was at Kunsthalle Bremen in 1976, covering works from 1962 to 1974. A traveling retrospective at Düsseldorf's Kunsthalle in 1986 was followed in 1991 by a retrospective at the Tate Gallery, London. In 1993, he received a major touring retrospective "Gerhard Richter: Malerei 1962–1993" curated by Kasper König, with a three-volume catalogue edited by Benjamin Buchloh, which entirely reinvented his career. Richter gained recognition in the U.S. in 1990 with the Saint Louis Art Museum's show of Baader-Meinhof (18 October 1977), later seen at the Lannan Foundation in Marina del Rey. His first North American retrospective was in 1998 at the Art Gallery of Ontario and the Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago. In 2002, a 40-year retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, traveled to the Art Institute of Chicago, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden. In 2016, he participated in the international exhibition Doppelgänger, curated by Sandra Mann, Ichiro Irie, Julia-Constance Dissel, Max Presneill, at the Torrance Art Museum, California. His work is included in permanent collections in the U.S., such as the Pérez Art Museum Miami. He has participated in several international art shows, including the Venice Biennale (1972, 1980, 1984, 1997, 2007) and Documenta V (1972), VII (1982), VIII (1987), IX (1992), and X (1997). In 2006, a Getty Center exhibition connected Richter's landscapes to Caspar David Friedrich's Romantic works, noting both artists used abstraction, expansiveness, and emptiness to express transcendent emotion. The Gerhard Richter Archive was established in 2005 in cooperation with the artist as an institute of the Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden. In 2020, Gerhard Richter established the Gerhard Richter Art Foundation, a non-profit dedicated to preserving his work and making it available for exhibitions. The first major exhibition of his work in Australia, Gerhard Richter: The Life of Images, was held by the Queensland Gallery of Modern Art in Brisbane from 14 October 2017 to 4 February 2018, including over 90 works, such as Atlas Overview, a 400-panel extract selected by Richter from the larger Atlas project now deemed too fragile for travel. In 2022, the Raphael Durazzo Gallery exhibited 2014: 20. November 2014, oil on colored photograph, 15 x 10 cm. Richter gained widespread fame during his 2005 retrospective, which declared his status as one of the most important artists of the 20th century; many now call him the best living painter, in part due to his exploration of painting at a time when many believed its medium was dying. He has received numerous awards, including the State Prize of North Rhine-Westphalia (2000), the Wexner Prize (1998), the Praemium Imperiale (Japan, 1997), the Golden Lion at the 47th Venice Biennale (1997), the Wolf Prize (Israel, 1994/5), the Goslarer Kaiserring Prize (1988), the Oskar Kokoschka Prize (Vienna, 1985), the Arnold Bode Prize (Kassel, 1981), and the Junger Western Art Prize (Germany, 1961). He was made an honorary citizen of Cologne in April 2007 and elected to the American Philosophical Society in 2012. Among his students at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf between 1971 and 1994 were Ludger Gerdes, Hans-Jörg Holubitschka, Bernard Lokai, Thomas Schütte, Thomas Struth, Katrin Kneffel, Michael van Ofen, and his second wife, Isa Genzken. He influenced Ellsworth Kelly, Christopher Wool, and Johan Andersson. He has also inspired writers and musicians; Sonic Youth used a painting for the cover of their 1988 album Daydream Nation, which Richter did not charge for, and the original over 7 meters (23 feet) square painting is now displayed in Sonic Youth's studio in NYC. Don DeLillo's short story "Baader-Meinhof" describes a meeting between two strangers at the MoMA in the room displaying 18 October 1977 (1988). Photographer Cotton Coulson described Richter as one of his favorite artists. For the last 18 years, Richter has ranked number one on a Kunstkompass scale of the most important world artists, made by German magazine Capital. Following an exhibition with Blinky Palermo at Galerie Heiner Friedrich in 1971, Richter ended his formal arrangement with the dealer in 1972; thereafter, Friedrich could only sell paintings he had already obtained under contract. In the following years, Richter exhibited with Galerie Konrad Fischer in Düsseldorf and Sperone Westwater in New York. Richter's primary dealer and representative gallery between 1985 and 2022 was Galerie Konrad Fischer, Düsseldorf.

A 7 metres (23 ft) square artwork is currently on display in Sonic Youth's studio in NYC. Don DeLillo's short story "Baader-Meinhof" features an encounter between two strangers at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, taking place in the room displaying 18 October 1977 (1988). Photographer Cotton Coulson described Gerhard Richter as "one of [his] favourite artists". For the last 18 years, Gerhard Richter has ranked as number one on a Kunstkompass scale of most important world artists, compiled by the German magazine Capital. Following an exhibition with Blinky Palermo at Galerie Heiner Friedrich in 1971, Richter's formal arrangement with the dealer ended in 1972, after which Friedrich could only sell paintings he had already obtained contractually. In subsequent years, Richter exhibited at Galerie Konrad Fischer in Düsseldorf and Sperone Westwater in New York. From 1985 to 2022, his primary dealer and representative gallery was Marian Goodman; since December 2022, he has been represented by David Zwirner Gallery. Today, museums own roughly 38% of Richter's works, including half of his large abstract paintings. By 2004, Richter's annual turnover reached $120 million. According to artnet, $76.9 million worth of Richter's work was sold at auction in 2010. As of 2012, at least 545 distinct Richter works had sold at auctions for over $100,000, with 15 selling for more than $10,000,000 between 2007 and 2012. Richter's paintings have been steadily moving out of Germany since the mid-1990s, although certain key German collectors—Frieder Burda, Josef Fröhlich, Georg Böckmann, and Ulrich Ströher—have retained their holdings. Richter's candle paintings were the first to achieve high auction prices; three months after his MoMA exhibition opened in 2001, Sotheby's sold his Three Candles (1982) for $5.3 million. In February 2008, his eldest daughter, Betty, sold her Kerze (1983) for £7,972,500 ($15 million), triple the high estimate, at Sotheby's in London. His 1982 Kerze (Candle) sold for £10.5 million ($16.5 million) at Christie's London in October 2011. In February 2008, Christie's London set a first record for Richter's "capitalist realism" pictures from the 1960s by selling Zwei Liebespaare (1966) for £7,300,500 ($14.3 million) to Stephan Schmidheiny. In 2010, the Weserburg modern art museum in Bremen, Germany, sold Richter's 1966 painting Matrosen (Sailors) at a Sotheby's auction in November, where John D. Arnold bought it for $13 million. Vierwaldstätter See, one of four views of Lake Lucerne painted by Richter in 1969, sold for £15.8 million ($24 million) at Christie's London in 2015. Another highly sought group is the Abstrakte Bilder series, especially those made after 1988, finished with a large squeegee rather than a brush or roller. At Pierre Bergé & Associés in July 2009, Richter's 1979 oil painting Abstraktes Bild sold for €95,000 ($136,000), exceeding its estimate. Richter's 1990 Abstraktes Bild achieved a record price of 7.2 million pounds, or about $11.6 million, at a Sotheby's sale in February 2011 to a bidder believed to be an agent for New York dealer Larry Gagosian. In November 2011, Sotheby's sold a group of colorful abstract canvases by Richter, including Abstraktes Bild 849-3, which set a record price for the artist at auction when Lily Safra paid $20.8 million and later donated it to the Israel Museum. Months later, a record $21.8 million was paid at Christie's for the 1993 painting Abstraktes Bild 798-3. Abstraktes Bild (809–4), one of Richter's abstract canvases from 1994, was sold by Eric Clapton at Sotheby's to a telephone bidder for $34.2 million in late 2012 (estimated to bring $14.1 million to $18.8 million). This was surpassed in May 2013 when his 1968 piece Cathedral Square, Milan sold for $37.1 million (£24.4 million) in New York. This was further exceeded in February 2015 when his 1986 painting Abstraktes Bild (599) sold for $44.52 million (£30.4 million) in London at Sotheby's Contemporary Evening Sale, becoming the highest price at auction for a piece of contemporary art at the time; Richter's record was later broken on 12 November 2013 when Jeff Koons' Balloon Dog (Orange) sold at Christie's in New York for US$58.4 million. When asked about such high art prices, Richter remarked, "It's just as absurd as the banking crisis. It's impossible to understand and it's daft!" In 2003, Gerald Fox produced a documentary on Richter's life. In 2007, Corinna Belz made a short film called Gerhard Richter's Window. In 2011, Belz released a feature-length documentary entitled Gerhard Richter Painting, focusing on the world's highest-paid living artist creating his large-scale abstract squeegee works in his studio. The 2018 drama film Never Look Away is inspired by Richter's life story. In 2016 and 2019, Richter collaborated again with Corinna Belz on two films based on his 2012 book Patterns. The earlier work, Richters Patterns, when shown, is paired with music by German composer Marcus Schmickler, and the later one with music by American composer Steve Reich, both performed by a live ensemble. The latter work is part of a larger two-section collaboration, Reich Richter Pärt, commissioned for the inaugural season at The Shed in the Hudson Yards development in Manhattan, New York City.
